meta.title: Property acquisition and cost recovery
meta.summary: Cost basis and capital versus repair, MACRS recovery periods and conventions, the MACRS tables, Section 179, bonus depreciation, real property, listed property and amortization.

videos.title: Basis and cost recovery
videos.take: A business asset's basis includes everything paid to get it ready for use; that cost is recovered over time

scenes.say: When a business buys an asset that lasts for years, it can't usually deduct the cost at once. It recovers it over time. First, what is the cost?
An asset's cost basis is everything paid to acquire it and get it ready for use: the price, sales tax, delivery and installation.

scenes.heading: Three ways to recover cost
scenes.say: Tangible property is depreciated, intangible property is amortized, and natural resources are depleted. Land is never depreciated, because it doesn't wear out.

scenes.heading: Capital or repair?
scenes.say: Costs that better, restore or adapt an asset are capitalized. Routine repairs are deducted. And under the de minimis safe harbor, a small business can deduct items costing $2,500 or less each.
Every dollar of depreciation reduces the asset's adjusted basis. That matters when you sell, as we'll see in Lecture 11.

scenes.q: Nora buys a printer for $3,800 plus $300 sales tax and $150 delivery. Her basis?
scenes.say: Quick check. Nora buys a printer for thirty-eight hundred dollars plus three hundred sales tax and one fifty delivery. What's her basis? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. Basis includes the tax and delivery: $4,250.

videos.title: MACRS: classes and conventions
videos.take: MACRS assigns each asset a recovery period, a method and a convention

scenes.say: The tax depreciation system is called MACRS. It doesn't ask how long your asset will really last. It tells you.

scenes.heading: Common MACRS classes
scenes.say: Cars, light trucks and computers are five-year property. Office furniture and most machinery are seven-year. Residential rental buildings are twenty-seven and a half years, and other buildings thirty-nine.

scenes.heading: Method
scenes.say: Personal property uses double-declining balance, switching to straight-line when that gives more. Buildings use straight-line. Salvage value is always ignored.

scenes.heading: Conventions
scenes.say: Conventions decide how much you get in the first and last year. Personal property assumes it was placed in service mid-year, the half-year convention. If more than forty percent of the year's purchases come in the last quarter, the mid-quarter convention applies. Buildings use mid-month.
Because of the half-year convention, five-year property is depreciated over six tax years: half a year at the start and half at the end.

scenes.q: Nora buys $6,000 of equipment in March and $5,000 in November, her only purchases in 2026. Which convention?
scenes.say: Quick check. Nora buys six thousand dollars of equipment in March and five thousand in November, her only purchases. Which convention applies? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. $5,000 of $11,000 is forty-five percent in the fourth quarter, over forty percent, so mid-quarter.

videos.title: Using the MACRS tables
videos.take: Multiply the asset's basis by the table percentage for its class and year

scenes.say: In practice, nobody computes double-declining balance by hand. You use the IRS tables. Here's how.

scenes.heading: Half-year convention, rates
scenes.say: The table gives a percentage for each year. Five-year property: twenty percent in year one, thirty-two in year two, nineteen point two in year three, eleven point five two in years four and five, and five point seven six in year six. Seven-year property starts at fourteen point two nine percent.

scenes.heading: Nora's cameras: $10,000, five-year, 2025
scenes.say: Nora bought $10,000 of cameras and lenses in 2025 and chose not to use bonus depreciation. Year one is twenty percent, $2,000. In 2026, year two, it's thirty-two percent: the $3,200 on her Schedule C. Adjusted basis falls to $4,800.
If you dispose of property before it's fully depreciated, take half of that year's amount under the half-year convention.

scenes.heading: If Nora sells the cameras in 2027
scenes.say: If Nora sells the cameras in 2027, the full year-three amount would be $1,920. She takes half: $960.

scenes.q: A $20,000 seven-year machine is placed in service in 2026 (half-year, no bonus). Year-one depreciation?
scenes.say: Quick check. A twenty thousand dollar seven-year machine is placed in service in 2026, with no bonus. What's year-one depreciation? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. Fourteen point two nine percent of $20,000 is $2,858.

videos.title: Section 179 expensing
videos.take: Section 179 lets a business expense up to $2,560,000 of equipment in 2026, limited to business income

scenes.say: Why depreciate over six years when you can deduct it all now? Section 179 lets businesses expense equipment immediately.

sub: in the year placed in service
scenes.say: Section 179 lets a business elect to deduct the cost of qualifying equipment, machinery, software and certain building improvements in the year it's placed in service.

scenes.heading: 2026 limits
scenes.say: For 2026 the maximum is $2,560,000. It's reduced dollar for dollar once purchases of qualifying property exceed $4,090,000, so it targets small and mid-sized businesses.
The deduction can't exceed taxable income from active businesses. Any excess carries forward. So Section 179 can't create a loss.

scenes.heading: 2027: Nora buys a $14,000 drone kit
scenes.say: In 2027, Nora buys a $14,000 professional drone kit and elects Section 179 for the full amount. Her business income is well above that, so she deducts all $14,000 that year, and there's nothing left to depreciate.

scenes.q: A business with $40,000 of taxable income elects $60,000 of Section 179. What is deductible this year?
scenes.say: Quick check. A business with forty thousand dollars of taxable income elects sixty thousand of Section 179. What's deductible this year? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. The deduction is limited to $40,000 of business income. The other $20,000 carries forward.

videos.title: Bonus depreciation
videos.take: 100% bonus depreciation is permanent for property acquired after January 19, 2025, and can create a loss

scenes.say: Bonus depreciation does what Section 179 does, but with no dollar cap and no income limit. The 2025 law made it permanent at one hundred percent.

scenes.heading: Bonus depreciation's path
scenes.say: The 2017 law allowed one hundred percent bonus depreciation, phasing down from 2023. The 2025 law restored one hundred percent permanently for property acquired after January nineteenth, 2025.

scenes.heading: Section 179 vs bonus
scenes.say: Section 179 has a dollar limit and an income limit, and you must elect it. Bonus depreciation has neither limit, can create a loss, and applies automatically unless you elect out for a whole class of property.

scenes.heading: Order of deductions
items: Then regular MACRS on any remainder
scenes.say: When both apply, take Section 179 first, then bonus on the remaining basis, then regular MACRS on anything left.

sub: or keep income for the QBI deduction
scenes.say: Why opt out? If you expect higher rates later, deductions are worth more then. Large deductions can also shrink your QBI deduction or waste credits.

scenes.q: In 2026 a startup with a loss buys $50,000 of equipment. Which gives a 2026 deduction that adds to its loss?
scenes.say: Quick check. In 2026, a startup with a loss buys fifty thousand dollars of equipment. Which method gives a deduction that adds to its loss? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Section 179 can't create a loss, but bonus depreciation can.

videos.title: Buildings, listed property and intangibles
videos.take: Buildings use straight-line and mid-month; listed property needs over 50% business use; Section 197 intangibles are amortized over 15 years

scenes.say: A few more cost recovery rules: for buildings, for property with personal use, and for intangibles.

scenes.heading: Erik's rental duplex, bought in July 2026
scenes.say: Erik buys a rental duplex in July for $325,000, of which $50,000 is land. The building's $275,000 basis is depreciated straight-line over twenty-seven and a half years: $10,000 a year. Under the mid-month convention, July counts as half a month, so 2026 gets five and a half months: $4,583.

sub: Cars and other property with personal use;
needs over 50% business use for MACRS
scenes.say: Listed property, mainly passenger cars, gets accelerated depreciation, Section 179 and bonus only if business use exceeds fifty percent. Otherwise it's straight-line. Passenger cars also face annual dollar caps, the so-called luxury auto limits.
Purchased intangibles, like goodwill, customer lists and non-compete agreements, are amortized straight-line over fifteen years.
Business start-up and organization costs can be deducted up to $5,000 each in the first year, phasing out above $50,000 of costs, with the rest amortized over a hundred and eighty months.

scenes.q: Nora buys a retiring photographer's client list for $30,000. Annual amortization?
scenes.say: Quick check. Nora buys a retiring photographer's client list for thirty thousand dollars. What's the annual amortization? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. A customer list is a Section 197 intangible: $30,000 over fifteen years is $2,000 a year.

warmup: Your business buys a $3,000 laptop. Should it be an expense this year or spread over its life? Argue both sides.
Matching says spread it; simplicity and incentives say expense it. Tax law does both: de minimis safe harbor (up to $2,500), Section 179, bonus, or MACRS.
acts: Capitalize or deduct? (a) Repainting the studio. (b) Adding a darkroom. (c) A $900 lens. (d) Replacing the studio's entire HVAC system.
(a) Deduct (maintenance). (b) Capitalize (betterment). (c) Deduct under the $2,500 de minimis safe harbor. (d) Capitalize (restoration of a unit of property).
Which convention? Purchases: $20,000 in February, $8,000 in October, $10,000 in December.
Compute MACRS for 2026–2028 on a $30,000 seven-year machine placed in service in 2026 (no bonus, no 179).
A business with $100,000 of taxable income buys $150,000 of equipment and elects $150,000 of Section 179. What is deductible, and what carries forward? What would bonus do instead?
Section 179 deduction $100,000; $50,000 carries forward. Bonus: $150,000 deducted, creating a $50,000 loss (NOL).
Erik's duplex: what depreciation in 2027 and 2028? What if it were an office building?
$10,000 each year (27.5 years). Office: 39 years, $275,000 ÷ 39 = $7,051 a year.
Nora pays $8,000 of legal and setup costs to start a second business. What can she deduct in year one if it starts on July 1?
case: Suppose that in 2026 Nora's business had made $30,000 of profit before any of these purchases, and she bought: a $14,000 drone kit (five-year) in May; a $4,500 studio lighting set (seven-year) in August; a $2,200 laptop in September; and an SUV for $45,000 in October that she'll use 70% for business. The couple's taxable income puts them in the 12% bracket.
Which items qualify for the de minimis safe harbor?
Which convention applies, and why does it matter?
Should Nora use Section 179, bonus or regular MACRS? Consider her income, SE tax and QBI deduction.
What special rules apply to the SUV?

Laptop: de minimis ($2,200). Q4 purchases: 45,000 of 63,500 depreciable cost = 71%, over 40%: mid-quarter for MACRS (property expensed under Section 179 is left out of the 40% test, so expensing the drone and lights would make it worse). Expensing everything would wipe out profit and SE tax but also the QBI deduction, and deductions are worth only 12% plus SE tax now; she might expense the drone kit and lighting and use regular MACRS on the SUV. SUV: listed property, 70% business use > 50%, so MACRS on the 70% business share; check the luxury auto caps (heavy SUVs over 6,000 lbs are exempt from the caps but have a lower Section 179 limit).
exam: Compare Section 179 and bonus depreciation in 2026 under four headings: dollar limit, income limit, election, and effect on a loss.
179: $2,560,000 limit (phase-out above $4,090,000); limited to business income; must elect; can't create a loss. Bonus: no limit; no income limit; automatic unless elected out; can create a loss.
A $50,000 five-year asset is placed in service in 2026; the taxpayer elects $20,000 of Section 179 and elects out of bonus. Compute 2026 and 2027 deductions.
